talking_points.text: These operations are the foundation for all later linear‑algebra concepts.
Geometrically, in R² and R³ vectors can be visualized as arrows starting at the origin.
A common mistake is to try to add vectors of different dimensions; the dimensions must match.
We will now see how these simple operations fit into the abstract definition of a vector space.
The axioms guarantee that any theorem proved from them applies to all listed examples.
Intuitively, the axioms say that vectors behave like arrows that can be moved and stretched consistently.
Example: In the space of 2×2 matrices, adding matrices and multiplying by scalars follows the same rules as for ordinary vectors.
A subtle point: the zero vector must be the same for both operations; some students forget to check this when verifying a new vector space.
Next we will examine special subsets of a vector space that are themselves vector spaces.
Subspaces let us focus on smaller, manageable parts of a vector space while preserving all structure.
The three‑condition test is sufficient because the other axioms are inherited from V.
Example: The set W={ (t,2t) | t∈ℝ } satisfies the three conditions, so it is a subspace of ℝ².
Common mistake: forgetting to verify that the zero vector belongs to W; the line y=2x+1 fails this test.
Understanding subspaces prepares us for concepts like span and basis.
The span captures everything we can reach using the given vectors and scalar multiples.
Intuition: think of the span as the “reach” of the vectors when you can stretch and add them.
Example: Vectors (1,0,0) and (0,1,0) in ℝ³ span the xy‑plane because any (x,y,0) can be written as x·(1,0,0)+y·(0,1,0).
A subtle point: the span of a single non‑zero vector is a line, not the whole space.
Later we will see how choosing independent vectors from a span leads to a basis.
Independence tells us that no vector in the set is redundant.
Intuitively, a basis is a minimal set of directions that can build every vector in the space.
Example: In ℝ², {(1,0),(0,1)} is independent and spans ℝ², so it is a basis; its size 2 is the dimension.
A common error is to assume any spanning set is a basis; independence must also be checked.
The standard basis of ℝⁿ consists of the n vectors with a single 1 and the rest 0, confirming that dim ℝⁿ = n.
We test whether a non‑trivial combination gives the zero vector.
Example: 3·(1,2) - (3,6) = (0,0); coefficients (3, -1) are not both zero, so the vectors are dependent.
Because they are multiples of each other, they span only a line, not the whole plane.
A subtle point: two vectors in ℝ² are independent precisely when they are not scalar multiples.
This exercise illustrates the definitions of dependence and span from the previous slides.
